summary: Home networks increasingly use IPv6, which could make reaching home devices from outside simpler, but only if names and addresses appear in the public DNS. This experimental document describes how a Home Naming Authority tells an outsourced DNS service to publish those names and addresses.

plainLanguage.summary: You want friends to find your home. Your home asks a public phone book keeper to list its name and number for you.

questions: publish home devices in public dns
subtitle: Let home networks publish device names and addresses in public DNS.

tldr.problem: Home networks want their devices accessible by name from the Internet, but managing DNS is complex, and running a resolver at home cannot handle external query load.
tldr.mechanism: The Home Naming Authority (HNA) in the home configures its domain zone and uses a control channel and zone transfer to synchronize with an outsourced DNS infrastructure that publishes the names.
tldr.outcome: Home devices become reachable by stable names while the home network avoids hosting its own authoritative DNS server. The system requires coordination between the HNA and outsourced provider.

today: RFC 9526 is an experimental specification published in January 2024. It provides the foundation for standardized home network DNS publication but remains experimental pending broader implementation and evaluation of deployment scenarios and configuration mechanisms.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
Homeowners increasingly want to reach devices on their home network from the Internet using stable, memorable names instead of IPv6 addresses. With IPv6, such direct access is simpler in principle, but names and addresses must appear in the public DNS.

Running an authoritative DNS server at home is impractical: home networks lack the capacity to handle query load from the Internet, and the HNA (Home Naming Authority) is a hidden primary, not publicly visible. This document describes how the HNA instructs a DNS Outsourcing Infrastructure (DOI) to publish and serve the home's zone on its behalf.
sections.plainLanguage: You want people on the Internet to find your home by name. You tell a big DNS company what your home should be called and what the address is, and they tell everyone else.

sections.title: The HNA Architecture
sections.content:
The system involves the Home Naming Authority (the HNA, typically the home router) that manages the zone, a Distribution Manager (DM) within the outsourced DOI that acts as a secondary server, and the Public Authoritative Servers that serve the zone to the Internet. The HNA acts as a hidden primary: it builds the zone locally, signs it with DNSSEC, and pushes it to the DM using standard DNS zone transfer mechanisms.

The HNA communicates with the DM over three channels: a Control Channel (DNS over TLS) to configure the delegation and exchange keying material, a Synchronization Channel (AXFR and IXFR over TLS) to push zone updates, and a Distribution Channel (internal to the DOI) that replicates the zone to public servers. The HNA is always the initiator; the DM contacts the HNA only to fetch zone updates.
sections.plainLanguage: Your router keeps a list of your devices. It tells an outsourced service what the list is. That service tells the public nameservers. The router only talks when it has new information.

sections.title: Control Channel Operations
sections.content:
The Control Channel is a DNS over TLS connection initiated by the HNA to the DM. It exchanges three kinds of information. First, the HNA sends a DNS AXFR (zone transfer) request to fetch a template zone from the DM, which contains the NS records and SOA values the HNA should use when building its zone. Second, the HNA sends a DNS UPDATE to provide the DNSSEC DS record to the DM for insertion into the parent zone, establishing the chain of trust. Third, the HNA sends another UPDATE to tell the DM the IP address where the DM should fetch zone updates (the Synchronization Channel address).

The Control Channel uses mutually authenticated TLS certificates. Both the HNA and DM authenticate each other, preventing unauthorized configuration changes. The channel is not persistent; it closes after information exchange and can be reopened as needed, especially if the HNA detects a renumbering event requiring a new IP address for the Synchronization Channel.
sections.plainLanguage: Your router calls the outsourced service over a secure line and says three things: here are the public nameservers you should list, here is my DNSSEC key, and here is where you should call to get updates.

sections.title: Synchronization and Zone Updates
sections.content:
The Synchronization Channel is a zone transfer mechanism between the HNA (primary) and DM (secondary). It operates over mutually authenticated TLS, separate from the Control Channel. The HNA runs a DNS server accepting zone transfer requests on port 853, and the DM connects to it to fetch zone updates using AXFR (full transfer) and IXFR (incremental transfer).

The HNA can also send DNS NOTIFY messages over the Control Channel to signal that updates are ready, prompting the DM to immediately perform a SOA query and initiate zone transfer. If NOTIFY is not sent, the DM checks the zone periodically based on the SOA REFRESH value. All zone content, including DNSSEC signatures, is handled by the HNA; the DM only distributes what it receives from the HNA.
sections.plainLanguage: Your router holds the real copy of the device list. The outsourced service calls your router to download updates. Your router can also poke the service and say 'I have changes for you.'

sections.title: Security and Privacy Considerations
sections.content:
The system protects the HNA's identity from external attackers by never advertising the HNA's address in the NS records of the public zone. The HNA remains hidden, reducing its attack surface from DDoS and other direct attacks. However, the HNA must trust the DM not to intercept or modify zone contents, and both must protect their mutual TLS certificates.

Names in the Public Homenet Zone are less volatile than IP addresses, so publishing stable names can ease device discovery. However, names are also less secure than IPv6 addresses for privacy purposes, as they are more memorable and easier to discover. Privacy considerations include the choice to publish IPv4 private addresses or ULAs; generally only Global Unicast Addresses (GUAs) should be published to prevent DNS rebinding attacks. DNSSEC is recommended to protect against spoofing.
sections.plainLanguage: Your router stays hidden, so attackers on the Internet cannot find it to attack. But the outsourced service must be trusted not to lose or break your zone.

sections.title: Deployment Scenarios
sections.content:
Two main deployment scenarios are described. CPE Vendor: a router manufacturer preconfigures the HNA with a certificate and domain name, enabling zero-configuration deployment—plug in the router and it automatically contacts the DOI. Agnostic CPE: an unconfigured router requires the home owner to buy a domain and configure the HNA with credentials, though this configuration can be provisioned via JSON to reduce manual entry.

In both cases, the provisioning of configuration is separate from the protocol specification and is expected to be handled by the CPE vendor, registrar, or outsourced DNS provider. Once configured, the protocol operates the same way regardless of how the initial credentials were established.
sections.plainLanguage: Some routers come preconfigured with a relationship with a DNS service and work immediately. Others require you to sign up first with your DNS provider and copy settings into the router.
